description: First-year Mechanical Engineering students who built this in the middle of our exams, using the time we’d set aside for studying. We’re not space experts. We just broke a hard problem into simple pieces and built a tool that makes lunar landing-site planning easier to see.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that lets a mission planner, educator or member of the public pick any point in four NASA Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar south pole (Malapert Massif, Haworth, Nobile Rim 1 and de Gerlache Rim) and get three answers at once: can we land here, will it have power, and can it talk to Earth.

For landing safety, it checks the slope and roughness of every 5 m cell under the landing circle using NASA’s LOLA elevation maps, with tolerances the user sets. For power and communications, it builds the terrain horizon in every direction out to 150 km and compares it hour by hour with Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons. It reports sunlit time, Earth-visible time, the longest darkness and the battery needed to survive it, plus the landing windows when the Sun and Earth are both up, and lets users compare sites side by side.

This addresses the challenge directly. Existing tools give Sun and Earth positions but are hard to use. Our app turns them into a visual comparison of sites and dates with Sun and Earth shown against the real horizon. At the south pole the Sun never rises more than a few degrees, so a nearby ridge can cut power or contact for days. Picking the right spot and the right dates decides whether a mission survives. We validated our results against NASA’s own maps: slope matches to within 0.001° (median) and sunlight correlates at 0.984.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers three questions for any point a user clicks in four NASA Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar south pole (Malapert Massif, Haworth, Nobile Rim 1, de Gerlache Rim): 1. Can we land here? (slope and roughness under the landing circle) 2. Will it have power? (is the Sun above the terrain horizon, hour by hour) 3. Can it talk to Earth? (is Earth above the terrain horizon). It reports sunlit %, Earth-visible %, both together, the longest darkness and the battery needed to survive it, and the landing windows when the Sun and Earth are both up. A time slider shows where the Sun and Earth are at any hour, and a table compares saved sites side by side.

HOW IT WORKS

Landing safety: slope and roughness are computed for every 5 m cell of NASA's LOLA elevation maps. The landing circle is the lander radius plus the landing uncertainty (100 m, matching Artemis III's targeting requirement). A spot passes only if every cell the circle touches is within tolerance and a plane fitted to the whole circle is within the footprint limits. The user sets all four tolerances, and the tool always reports what the spot actually measures, because what counts as landable depends on the mission. At NASA's 8 deg tilt limit with a 100 m circle, none of the 10,000 spots we tested in our Malapert map tile passed - which is exactly why site choice matters.

Horizon: for every direction, the tool finds the highest terrain angle out to 150 km, correcting for the Moon's curvature. A quick mode uses the 80 m polar map; a precise mode adds the 5 m map nearby.

Sun and Earth: positions come from NASA JPL Horizons. One hourly table per region is precomputed and mathematically moved to any clicked point, so the app works offline and responds instantly. The Sun counts as visible when its centre is above the horizon; Earth counts as visible when any part of its disc is, matching NASA's own rule.

Validation: our slope matches NASA's slope maps to within 0.001 deg (median, 79 million cells), our horizon formula is within 0.017 deg of exact 3D geometry, and our sunlight and Earth-visibility figures correlate with NASA's illumination maps at 0.984 and 0.97-1.00.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Today, checking a landing site means combining separate maps and an ephemeris tool with a complicated interface. This puts landing safety, power and communications for one landing circle into a single click, with honest numbers and stated limits. Mission planners can screen sites and dates quickly; teachers and the public can see why the south pole is so hard.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

NASA already publishes illumination maps. What is new here is one tool that combines landing safety, power and comms for a user-chosen landing circle, with adjustable tolerances, a solar-panel mast-height trade-off (at our Malapert test point a 10 m mast raises sunlight from 54.5% to 100% for the month) and battery sizing.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED AND LIMITS

Hazards smaller than a 5 m cell are invisible; the Sun is treated as a point; Earth in view is necessary but not sufficient for comms (Deep Space Network availability is not modelled); map slope error is 1.5-2.5 deg; our Sun/Earth data covers about 14 months versus NASA's 18.6-year averages.

NEXT STEPS

Rover traverse paths between sites, the Sun as a disc, and the full 18.6-year cycle.

TOOLS

Python, Streamlit, Plotly, NumPy, pandas, rasterio, requests. Data: NASA LOLA (PGDA products 78, 90, 69) and the NASA JPL Horizons API.
